messages.subject: Re: Increase Iteration
messages.body_plain:
I would suggest adding priors to the lower and upper bound parameters as the 4PL is very difficult to estimate. Otherwise, you could try increasing the iteration count to something higher, though I would not expect this to solve the problem as the lack of EM termination suggests the log-likelihood/posterior is quite flat.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: NaN for S_X2 in Itemfit function
messages.subject_clean: NaN for S_X2 in Itemfit function
messages.body_plain:
Low N combined with sparse expected values will result in 0 df, particularly for polytomous response models. You can adjust the threshold of the expectation collapsing criteria, but in general I would not advise doing this as it can result in very poor p-value behaviour.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Integrating multiple Imputations from "mice" to "mirt"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

I would generally advise against using mirt's MI methods for missing data (they are model-based and inherently conservative), so MI would be the way to go. In terms of the code you would likely run the 20 models, store them as a list, and pool the results using Rubin's method. I have added some support for this via the function averageMI() (https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/docs/reference/averageMI.html). Does that help?

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Confirmatory mirt vs. target rotation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I don't think you did anything wrong, it's just that the model shows a suboptimal fit to the data (hence it's probably not the best data-generating model). Part of the issue likely is because of the sheer number of weakly defined factors (with only three indicators), but there may be other reasons for the poor fit too, of course. You might consider taking item subsets first to see how well the unidimensionality assumption holds in each factor, check the item/model fit, and see if there are local problems that could be fixed. Otherwise, this becomes a theory-centric problem and you may need to think of other causal reasons the select model does not fit the data well. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: item parameter estimates obtained from mirt()
messages.subject_clean: item parameter estimates obtained from mirt()
messages.body_plain:
The setup looks correct to me, though note that ey is not on the same scale as ex due to the mean-var shift in the trait distribution (hence, the need for equating, which can be done via the plink package [e.g., https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/read.mirt.html] or using the multipleGroup() function for concurrent equating).

Regarding your questions:

>
> 1. Is the estimation method by default marginal maximum likelihood?

Yes, and if item prior distributions are included this becomes marginal maximum a posteriori.

>
> 2. For dentype: 'Gaussian' (default) assumes a multivariate Gaussian distribution with an
> associated mean vector and variance-covariance matrix. Is the "associated mean vector and variance-covariance matrix" by default standard restrictions?

Yes, and most often set to 0-1.

>
> 3. Any parameter I should use but did not include in my code?

Looks fine to me as this is the building blocks for many equating algorithms.

Phil

>
> Thank you very much!

messages.subject: Re: Jin and Wang (2014) via createItem()
messages.body_plain:
I believe you can do this, but the setup will be quite clunky. What I would do in this case is

- Set up a customTheta input and estimate the model as a multidimensional IRT model with k=2 factors. One factor is intended to be the trait (Theta[,1], say) while the other column is independent to define the integration grid for w
- Define a custom prior distribution to define the associated marginalization of the integrals (in Jin and Wang they assume a log-normal for w)
- Re-write the createItem() code such that w <- Theta[,2], and carry forward in that respect to ensure it is properly vectorized
- Ensure that the proper variance terms are estimate for the random effects found in Theta

Not exactly elegant, of course, and could be error prone. Might be best to try this type of model in Stan as I can foresee issues during estimation which could cause the estimator to crash.

Phil

On Thu, Dec 9, 2021 at 7:53 AM Chhavi Mittal Goyal <mittal....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi All
>
> I am a novice when it comes to both R and Item response theory models. I am working with a set of polytomous situational items having SME reviewed key from 1 to 4 (4 being the most appropriate response). Not all the items are presented to my testtakers, but they receive a random subset of the items. There would be some overlapping items, but no anchor items. I want to standardize my item bank, I currently have 99 items, and I am hoping to retain about 40-50 good items. I have the following queries:
>
> 1.       Is Multidimensional GPCM model the correct model for this data? If not, please suggest the alternative model.

Nobody here can answer that as it is domain and content specific.

>
> 2.       When I run the command > mod1<-mirt(data,1,itemtype=”gpcm”) followed by the command for coef(mod1) I am unable to interpret the output. What is meant by the terms ak0, ak1, ak2,ak3,d0?

That's one approach, particularly when using the information criteria.

It's unlikely the data are MCAR, more likely MAR, but even at that it's an assumption that you would need to think about and justify.

messages.subject: Re: Item information matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hynek,

On Tue, Mar 22, 2022 at 9:04 AM Hynek Cígler <cigler...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello,
> I have several questions concerning the item information matrix and selection criteria used in mirt and mirtCAT. These could be elementary questions for somebody here, but I am - as a non-statistician - struggling :-) All the questions are related to a confirmatory multidimensional model with correlated traits, where each item has only one or two non-zero loadings.
>
> First of all, I have a problem conceptually understanding what do the off-diagonal elements of the item information matrix (IIM) represent. Is it un uncertainty related to the difference (or trade-off) between two thetas estimates?

The off-diagonal elements have to do with whether the item correlates with both traits (i.e., has non-zero slopes for each), in which case the item will measures something about more than one variable (diagonal terms) with some degree of shared information (off-diagonal). Items containing only one unique loading will have zers everywhere except their respective diagonal.

>
>
> Second, I want to estimate information in the direction of the single dimension. Therefore, the angle between this single direction and my dimension is zero. Thus the weight of a particular element in IIM will be 1 (as the cos(0) = 1 = r). But what about the other dimensions? Will these weights be zero, or should I add the factor correlation?

You would want set the weights of the other dimensions to zero, though rarely is this something that I recommend doing (unless you are searching for some maximal multidimensional information location, in which case MDIFF is the answer).

> An example: I have two traits correlated r = 0.5. An item has the two factor loadings a_1 = 0.6 and a_2 = 0.7. The item information matrix would be
>
>
> If I consider the angle 0 and 90 (r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = 0}), the weighted IIM would be
>
> However, the traits are correlated, r = .5. Therefore, the question is whether angles 0 and 90 degrees are admissible. Shouldn't I use angles r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = .5}, where the second angle represents the correlation of both traits? In such a case, IIM would be equal to
>
>
> The latter gives me a sense as off-diagonals are related to discriminations between traits, and therefore, they are not zero. With highly correlated traits, off-diagonals elements will be close to zero, representing the inability to discriminate between correlated dimensions, and vice versa. However, an item could add information even in the factor with zero loading in the latter. Is it correct?

This sounds correct from what I gather you're trying to do. Unidimensional items still provide information about other latent traits if indeed the traits are modeled to be correlated.

>
> The other question is related to item selection criteria. I did not find any documentation of them, so I ask here:

Did you refer to the associated JSS article?

> D-rule (IIM determinant) - this maximalize the ability to estimate each trait and discriminate between them, as it uses the whole information matrix?

Yes, and analogously minimizes the expected measurement error by way of the determinant geometry.

> T-rule (IIm diagonal) - this maximalize only the ability to estimate each trait, as it does not consider the off-diagonal elements?

Correct.

> A-rule (covariance matrix diagonal) - similar to T-rule, but work with an error matrix (inversed item information matrix)?

Yes, and can behave differently (arguably, more optimally) when user-defined weights are included.

> E-rule: I do not understand here. In mirt help, it is written: "the minimum value of the information matrix". Why does anybody want to use that?

You generally don't, unless you're looking to uniformly minimize the general variance of the trait estimates.

> W-rule: the same here. What means "the weighted information criteria"? Shouldn't be here a "weighted information matrix"?

Is there a difference? Weights are applied to the information matrix to result in a scalar.

>
> Finally, for D-rule, T-rule, and E-rule, it is written "potentially weighted matrix". The matrix is therefore weighted using factors correlation matrix, right?

Not quite, these are based on user-defined weights, where you may be working with a multidimensional test but really only want to select items that pertain to a specific dimension (such as the general factor in a bi-factor model). HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
It should also be noted that using update() is a viable option, which contains better documentation in the update.trellis(). See below for an example, which modifies the ylab of the graphical object:

###

library(mirt)

mod <- mirt(Science, 1)

(plt <- itemplot(mod, 1))

# see ?update.trellis
update(plt, ylab = expression(Prob(theta)))
###

Use of the latticeExtra package is often quite useful here too if users are interested in adding additional layers().

Phil

messages.subject: A question about a simulation test with small sample size
messages.subject_clean: A question about a simulation test with small sample size
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am planning to perform a simulation test to find out how many responses I need to collect so that the model RMSEA is less than a certain threshold. I have been reading articles here and there about monte carlo simulation, and I am not sure if I am on the right track. I would be grateful if someone can give me some advice/feedback about my steps here.

Basically, I collected some pilot data (n=15) from a questionnaire with 100 items (6 questions with 7 categories, and the rest with 5 categories). So, I most likely ended with a multidimensional gpcm. With such a small dataset, I did an exploratory factor analysis using Jamovi and it figures it is about three factors (skeptical, but I assume it is ok and ran with it).

So now, assuming that this is a 3-dimensional gpcm model, I use mirt to create a model with 15 responses and evaluate it using M2. Unsurprisingly, the RMSEA is 0.1993603.

Now, assuming that the model is appropriate, I would like to find out how many samples I need to bring the RMSEA down below a certain threshold. So, I used simdata to generate data (using model = the_naive_model_with_15_samples), I tried 250, 500, and 1000 samples, I can see the RMSEA is coming down quite a lot (n=500 is 0.006, and n=1000 is 0.003, however with p-value > 0.1 though).

So my question is, is this an acceptable way to get a sense of how many responses I need to collect from the pilot data?

 Any comment would be much appreciated...thanks! 🙏
